'''Nina Claire Snaith''' is a British mathematician at the [[University of Bristol]] working in [[random matrix theory]] and [[quantum chaos]].

==Education==
Snaith was educated at the [[University of Bristol]] where she received her PhD in 2000<ref name=PhDsniath>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Bristol|title=Random matrix theory and zeta functions|first= Nina Claire|last=Snaith|date=2000|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.322610}}|oclc=53552484}}</ref> for research supervised by [[Jonathan Keating]].<ref name=mathgene/>

==Career and research==
In 1998, Snaith and her then adviser [[Jonathan Keating]] conjectured a value for the leading coefficient of the asymptotics of the moments of the [[Riemann zeta function]]. Keating and Snaith's guessed value for the constant was based on random-matrix theory, following
a trend that started with [[Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture]]. Keating's and Snaith's work extended works<ref name="Conrey Gonek 2001 p. ">{{cite journal | last=Conrey | first=J. B. | last2=Gonek | first2=S. M. | title=High moments of the Riemann zeta-function | journal=Duke Mathematical Journal | volume=107 | issue=3 | date=2001-04-15 | issn=0012-7094 | doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-01-10737-0 | page=| arxiv=math/9902162 }}</ref> by [[Brian Conrey]], Ghosh, and Gonek, also conjectural, based on number theoretic [[heuristic]]s; Conrey, Farmer, Keating, Rubinstein, and Snaith later conjectured the lower terms in the asymptotics of the moments.<ref name="Conrey Farmer Keating Rubinstein 2005 Snaith">{{cite journal | last=Conrey | first=J. B. | last2=Farmer | first2=D. W. | last3=Keating | first3=J. P. | last4=Rubinstein | first4=M. O. | last5=Snaith | first5=N. C. | title=Integral moments of L-functions | journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society | volume=91 | issue=01 | date=2005 | issn=0024-6115 | doi=10.1112/S0024611504015175 | pages=33–104| arxiv=math/0206018 }}</ref> Snaith's work appeared in her doctoral thesis ''Random Matrix Theory and zeta functions''.<ref name=mathgene>{{MathGenealogy}}</ref>

Snaith is currently Professor of Mathematical Physics at the University of Bristol.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nina Snaith's Home Page |website=Department of Mathematics |publisher=University of Bristol |url=https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~mancs/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bristol.ac.uk/people/person/Nina-Snaith-f93497f4-b355-4b92-95dc-8fb7f2fb6404/ |title=Professor Nina Snaith |website=University of Bristol: Our People |access-date=2023-05-20}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
In 2008, Snaith was awarded the London Mathematical Society's [[Whitehead Prize]].

In 2014, she delivered the annual [[Hanna Neumann]] Lecture to honour the achievements of women in mathematics.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hanna Neumann Lecturer |url=https://austms.org.au/special-interest-groups/wimsig/hanna-neumann-lecturer/ |access-date=20 May 2023 |archive-date=20 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230520125232/https://austms.org.au/special-interest-groups/wimsig/hanna-neumann-lecturer/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Snaith is the daughter of mathematician {{ill|Victor Snaith|de}} and sister of mathematician and musician [[Dan Snaith]], mostly known by his artistic names Manitoba, Caribou, and Daphni.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Jardine | first = J. F. | author-link = Rick Jardine

 | pages = 1041–1058
 | title = Victor Percy Snaith, 1944–2021
 | volume = 55}}</ref>
